title: The forgotten undo
prompt: If you delete `path.remove(path.size() - 1)` from the subsets template, what happens?
options: Choices pile up in `path` across loop iterations — results contain over-long, wrong subsets
Only the empty subset is produced
explanation: `path` is ONE shared list threaded through the whole recursion. Every add must be mirrored by a remove on the way back out, or state leaks between branches.

title: Template: permutations with used[]
explanation: A permutation is complete when it uses every element. Record a copy, because `path` keeps changing. Order matters, so every position may take any unused element: loop from 0 and skip used ones. Both mutations need undoing, the `path.remove` and `used[i] = false`.

title: Drill: combinations C(n, k)
prompt: From memory (choose/explore/un-choose with a `start` index): return all combinations of `k` numbers chosen from `1..n`.

solution.explanation: The `start` index keeps each path strictly increasing, so every set of k numbers is built exactly once. Stopping at size k turns the subsets tree into a combinations tree. There are C(n, k) results, each copied in O(k): O(k·C(n, k)) time, O(k) recursion depth.

hints: A combination doesn't care about order, so [1,2] and [2,1] are the same. How do you make sure you only ever build one of them?
Backtrack with a `start` value: loop `i` from `start` to `n`, and recurse with `i + 1` so later picks are always larger.
Record `new ArrayList<>(path)` when `path.size() == k`, then return. Un-choose with `path.remove(path.size() - 1)`.

title: Allowing reuse
prompt: In Combination Sum, each candidate may be chosen **any number of times**. Inside `for (int i = start; i < nums.length; i++)`, which recursive call is correct?
explanation: Passing `i` lets the next level pick `nums[i]` again while still ignoring earlier indices. `i + 1` forbids reuse, which is the rule for Combination Sum II. Passing `0` or `start` lets later levels go back to earlier indices, so `[2,2,3]` would also appear as `[2,3,2]` and `[3,2,2]`.

title: Template: skip duplicates at the same depth
prompt: Complete Subsets II: `nums` has already been sorted.
explanation: `i > start` means "not the first candidate in this loop," so only a repeated value in the same loop is skipped. The first copy still recurses, which is how `[2,2]` gets built. `i + 1` uses each index at most once. Without sorting first, equal values wouldn't sit next to each other and the check would miss them.

title: Drill: all binary strings
prompt: From memory: return all binary strings of length `n` in the order produced by choosing '0' before '1' at each position (e.g. n=2 → ["00","01","10","11"]). Backtrack with a StringBuilder: append, recurse, deleteCharAt.

solution.explanation: The same skeleton as subsets, with a length base case instead of recording at every call. `deleteCharAt(length - 1)` is the un-choose for a StringBuilder, so the next branch starts from the right prefix. There are 2ⁿ strings of length n, so O(n·2ⁿ) time including building each string, and O(n) recursion depth.

hints: Each position is a choice between two characters. How do you build a string one choice at a time and then try the other choice?
Recurse with a shared `StringBuilder`: when its length reaches n, record `path.toString()` and return.
For each of '0' and '1': `path.append(c); backtrack(n, path); path.deleteCharAt(path.length() - 1);`
